+## How to pass data between ASO resources
+
+You can pass data from one ASO resource to another without hardcoding values. If the source resource can export a value to a `ConfigMap` (see below), configure it to do so, then have the consuming resource read that value with a `...FromConfig` field.
+
+For example, a `UserAssignedIdentity` can export its `clientId` and `principalId` to a `ConfigMap`:
+
+```yaml
+apiVersion: managedidentity.azure.com/v1api20181130
+kind: UserAssignedIdentity
+metadata:
+  name: sampleuserassignedidentity
+  namespace: default
+spec:
+  owner:
+    name: aso-sample-rg
+  operatorSpec:
+    configMaps:
+      clientId:
+        name: identity-settings
+        key: clientId
+      principalId:
+        name: identity-settings
+        key: principalId
+```
+
+A `RoleAssignment` can then read the `principalId` from that `ConfigMap`:
+
+```yaml
+apiVersion: authorization.azure.com/v1api20200801preview
+kind: RoleAssignment
+metadata:
+  name: fee8b6b1-fe6e-481d-8330-0e950e4e6b86 # Should be UUID
+  namespace: default
+spec:
+  owner:
+    name: aso-sample-rg
+    group: resources.azure.com
+    kind: ResourceGroup
+  principalIdFromConfig:
+    name: identity-settings
+    key: principalId
+  roleDefinitionReference:
+    armId: /subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/roleDefinitions/b24988ac-6180-42a0-ab88-20f7382dd24c
+```
+
+The exporting resource won't move to `Ready=True` until the data has been written, so the consuming resource can rely on the value being present. For resources that support references to other ASO resources directly (such as `roleDefinitionReference` above), you can also point at the Kubernetes resource instead of a raw ARM ID.

+When installing ASO with Argo CD, point Argo at the ASO Helm chart repository rather than at the chart directory in the git source. Argo CD fetches and templates the published Helm chart, which includes generated templates such as the `azureserviceoperator-manager-role` `ClusterRole`. Pointing Argo at the git source directory instead can miss those generated templates, leaving the controller pod unable to start.
+

+kind: Application
+spec:
+  source:
+    repoURL: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Azure/azure-service-operator/main/v2/charts
+    targetRevision: v2.8.0
+    chart: azure-service-operator

+```

+
+### How should I schedule ASO when running on AKS?
+
+ASO doesn't set any AKS-specific node affinity by default, because ASO is supported on many kinds of Kubernetes cluster, not just AKS. On AKS, you may want to keep the ASO controller off your user node pools (or prefer your system node pool) by configuring affinity yourself.
+
+For example, to prefer scheduling the ASO controller on the system node pool, add a preferred node affinity to the `azureserviceoperator-controller-manager` deployment:
+
+```yaml
+affinity:
+  nodeAffinity:
+    preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
+    - weight: 1
+      preference:
+        matchExpressions:
+        - key: kubernetes.azure.com/mode
+          operator: In
+          values:
+          - system
+```
+
+Use `preferred` rather than `required` so that ASO can still be scheduled on clusters (or node pools) that don't have this label.
+

 There are a lot of similarities between ASO and Crossplane. They do similar things and have similar audiences. You can see some of this discussed [here](https://github.com/Azure/azure-service-operator/issues/1190).

+### 3. (Optional) Use a dedicated replica as the source
+
+To avoid running logical replication directly against your production primary,
+you can stand up a dedicated PostgreSQL replica and point Materialize at it
+instead. The replica uses PostgreSQL's native [logical
+replication](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/logical-replication.html)
+to receive changes from the primary, and Materialize then reads from the
+replica using its own publication.
+
+{{< note >}}
+This is an optional topology. It adds a second PostgreSQL instance and an extra
+hop of replication, so weigh the reduced load on the primary against the extra
+operational overhead and replication lag.
+{{< /note >}}
+
+1. Provision a PostgreSQL instance to serve as the replica, and configure it as
+   described in steps 1 and 2 above: set `wal_level` to `logical`, and create a
+   replication user.
+
+1. On the **primary**, create a publication for the tables you want to
+   replicate to the replica:
+
+    ```postgres
+    CREATE PUBLICATION mz_replica_pub FOR TABLE <table1>, <table2>;
+    ```
+
+1. On the **replica**, create a subscription to the primary's publication:
+
+    ```postgres
+    CREATE SUBSCRIPTION mz_replica_sub
+      CONNECTION 'host=<primary_host> port=5432 dbname=<dbname> user=<replication_user> password=<password>'
+      PUBLICATION mz_replica_pub;
+    ```
+
+    The subscription copies the initial table data and then streams ongoing
+    changes from the primary.
+
+1. On the **replica**, create a separate publication for Materialize to read
+   from. Materialize creates its own replication slot on the instance you
+   connect to, so the publication must exist on the replica:
+
+    ```postgres
+    CREATE PUBLICATION mz_source FOR TABLE <table1>, <table2>;
+    ```
+
+1. Verify that changes on the primary are reaching the replica before creating
+   the source in Materialize.
+
+When you [create the connection](#2-create-a-connection) in Materialize, use
+the replica's host and port instead of the primary's, and reference the
+publication you created on the replica (`mz_source` in the example above).
+
+{{< warning >}}
+- Materialize creates a replication slot on the instance it connects to. Point
+  the source at the replica, not the primary, or you will reintroduce load on
+  the primary.
+- Changes are only visible to Materialize after they have been applied on the
+  replica, so expect additional replication lag compared to sourcing directly
+  from the primary.
+- The replica must have `wal_level` set to `logical` and enough
+  `max_wal_senders` and `max_replication_slots` capacity for both the
+  subscription from the primary and the slot created by Materialize.
+- Schema changes on the primary must be propagated to the replica before
+  Materialize observes them; see the [known
+  limitations](/sql/create-source/postgres/#known-limitations).
+{{< /warning >}}
+

+## Pausing and resuming subscriptions
+
+Each subscription has an **enabled** state. You can pause a subscription by toggling it off in the subscriptions list or on the subscription's detail view. A paused subscription keeps its configuration but stops delivering on its schedule – it is not deleted, and you can resume it at any time with the same toggle.
+
+Pausing is distinct from deleting: deleting a subscription soft-deletes it, while a paused subscription is fully reversible.
+
+### Automatic disabling
+
+PostHog automatically pauses a subscription when its delivery target becomes permanently invalid – for example, when the Slack integration backing a Slack subscription is removed, or when the subscription's delivery channel is not supported. When this happens, the subscription is set to disabled, an activity record is written, and the subscription owner receives an email explaining why.
+
+To resume delivery, fix the underlying issue first (for example, reconnect the Slack integration) and then re-enable the subscription. Re-enabling triggers an immediate delivery so you can confirm the fix worked. If the underlying issue is still unresolved, re-enabling is rejected with an error explaining what needs to be fixed.
+
 ## Testing subscriptions
 
 You can manually trigger a test delivery for any subscription. Click the **...** menu on a subscription in the list and select **Test delivery**. This immediately sends the subscription content to the configured target (email or Slack channel) without waiting for the next scheduled delivery.
 
 This is useful for verifying that the subscription is configured correctly and the content looks as expected.
+
+Test delivery is not available for paused subscriptions. Re-enable the subscription first, then send a test delivery.

+## Selecting columns to sync
+
+By default, PostHog syncs every column of each table you import. To keep columns out of PostHog (for example, PII columns), you can choose which columns to sync:
+
+- **During setup:** On the **Select tables to import** step, click **Columns** on a table and check the columns you want to sync.
+- **After setup:** On the source's schemas tab, click **Columns** on a table, or open the table's configuration page and use the **Columns** section.
+
+Primary key columns and the active incremental field are always synced, even if you don't select them, so incremental syncs and deduplication keep working. Selecting no columns syncs only those required columns.

+Columns you disable are removed from the table's schema in PostHog, so they won't appear in HogQL queries. +.. setting:: database_engine_callback
+
+``database_engine_callback``
+~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
+
+Default: :const:`None` (no callback).
+
+A callable that is invoked with the SQLAlchemy engine immediately after it is
+created by the database result backend. This allows you to perform custom
+engine configuration, such as registering connection-level event listeners or
+setting pragmas::
+
+    from sqlalchemy import event
+
+    def register_do_connect(engine):
+        @event.listens_for(engine, 'do_connect')
+        def on_connect(dialect, conn_rec, cargs, cparams):
+            cparams['application_name'] = 'celery'
+
+    app.conf.database_engine_callback = register_do_connect
+
+The callback may also be given as a dotted import path string, which is
+resolved at initialization time::
+
+    app.conf.database_engine_callback = 'myapp.db:register_do_connect'
+
+If the resolved value is not callable, an :exc:`~celery.exceptions.ImproperlyConfigured`
+exception is raised.
+
+The callback can also be passed directly as the ``engine_callback`` keyword
+argument to the :class:`~celery.backends.database.DatabaseBackend` constructor,
+in which case it takes precedence over this setting::
+
+    DatabaseBackend('db+sqlite:///results.db', app=app, engine_callback=register_do_connect)
+

+#### Transform data with `add_map`
+
+`add_map` attaches a function that is applied to each individual data item (for example, a dict or
+row) as it is extracted from the resource. The function receives one item and must return the
+transformed item. Use it to rename or drop fields, compute new values, anonymize records, or
+otherwise reshape data before it is normalized and loaded.
+
+```py
+import dlt
+
+@dlt.resource
+def users():
+    yield {"id": 1, "email": "jane@example.com", "created_at": "2024-01-01"}
+    yield {"id": 2, "email": "john@example.com", "created_at": "2024-01-02"}
+
+def add_email_domain(user):
+    user["email_domain"] = user["email"].split("@")[-1]
+    return user
+
+# apply the transformation to every item yielded by the resource
+users_with_domain = users().add_map(add_email_domain)
+```
+
+You can chain `add_map` with other item-level transformations such as `add_filter` and
+`add_yield_map`, and call it on a resource instance obtained from a source (for example,
+`source.my_resource.add_map(...)`).
+
